His reputation as a sober thinker, safe writer, and sound lawyer is irretrievably damaged, his contributions become too dull to attract editors, and he is eventually forced into a post far beneath his earlier prospects.

l: Merman's household finances, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Merman's household finances are strained by his unprofitable controversy; capital is nearly exhausted, Julia cuts wants and sells a wedding jewel for rent, and Merman's low-level post becomes necessary.

l: Merman's bitterness and decline, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Merman's bitterness and decline is a chronic, irrevocable deterioration caused by prolonged disappointment and resistance. His certainty and resentment grow amid criticism and ridicule; he becomes inflexible, loses friends and opportunities, and suffers mental weakening. Though he later speaks less and admits errors, the damage endures.

l: Lentulus, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Lentulus is a man remembered as fair in society: well-looking, polite, acceptable, sociable at clubs and dinners, and supported by a business in which he does nothing. Benevolent and free from envy, hatred, and malice, he nevertheless has vast, ignorant confidence in his own rambling originality. He dismisses poets, philosophers, and scientific thought as mistaken, knows little of particular poets or doctrines, and defines poetry as artificial language expressing unreal sentiments. He claims to compose superior poetry spontaneously, considers writing on philosophic thinking, and expects his views on electricity to offend the scientific world. Yet he never clearly develops these reformative ideas; his silence leaves his vague, addled conclusions harmless.

l: vanity and arrogance, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Vanity and arrogance are complacent self-estimate unwarranted by performance, sometimes hidden by silence or apparent neutrality that avoids testing. Though compatible with worthy character, unchecked conceit becomes cruel and self-justifying; wider reason must restrain these fierce inner beasts.

l: society, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: misjudges Lentulus [as an unopinionated, useful social listener] Society mistakes Lentulus for an agreeable, unopinionated man who can serve as an admiring listener or vote for others' friends. Lentulus believes that the confused condition of society reveals widespread errors in thinking, marriage, social arrangements, and moral schemes.

l: poets, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: are_admired_by narrator [with grateful admiration across all ages] Lentulus assents to praise of celebrated poets with visible reserve, as though he knows that they are merely versifiers. He knows little of particular poets but believes that poetry should use true ideas and that the world has no notion what poetry will become; the narrator concludes that Lentulus cannot eclipse or fundamentally revise the poets.

l: philosophers, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Lentulus treats philosophers as mistaken and suggests that all thinking before his own has been an elaborate error. He names Plato, Robert Owen, and Dr Tuffle as equally wrong, despite lacking a developed knowledge of philosophical systems.

l: poetics, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Lentulus implies that existing poetics is inadequate and that he could establish principles for a new kind of poetry. The narrator initially suspects that Lentulus possesses a revolutionary treatise on poetics, but learns that Lentulus has neither written such a work nor clearly formulated its principles.

l: philosophic thinking, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Lentulus claims that philosophic thinking has been fundamentally mistaken until the beginning of his own reflections. His proposed insights range loosely over logic, miracles, marriage, electricity, motives, and causes, but remain unwritten or insufficiently organized.

l: human error, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_subject_to Lentulus [through his mistaken confidence in private insights] Lentulus regards human error as pervasive in poetry, philosophy, science, social institutions, and ordinary reasoning. He treats his unfamiliarity with established doctrines as evidence that he can correct the errors of previous thinkers, though the narrator sees his conclusions as blind denials and disjointed commonplaces.

l: heterodoxy, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_regarded_as power [by Lentulus, in itself] Lentulus regards heterodoxy as a power in itself and mistakes his lack of acquaintance with established doctrines for creative dissidence. His heterodox opinions remain mostly private because he lacks the words to turn them into a system or gather followers.

l: human imagination, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Powerful imagination begins as intense inward representation, not confusion of fact with fancy. Fed by susceptibility to minutiae of experience, it uses definite knowledge for creative inward construction, combines ideal and associative power with clear ordinary reality, and does not measure posterity by present poverty.

l: Hinze, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Hinze is an Alsatian man from a family settled in England for more than one generation. Well off and gentlemanly educated, he seeks above all to stand well with the justly distinguished and to present himself correctly. He cultivates low-toned tete-a-tete, praises wisdom, elevates ordinary remarks, and cites distinguished opinions. His deference serves neither ambition nor gain, including with Tulpian, and he has no doubleness toward Felicia. Lacking genuine judgments or lasting impressions, he is not consciously false or fairly a hypocrite.

l: Felicia, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Felicia is a clever, sensible, vivacious, kindly-disposed woman who helps her distinguished husband and welcomes visitors. She finds Babes in the Wood enchanting; speaking with Hinze, his reverence embarrasses her, and she resists being treated as an oracle.

l: Shakspere, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_expected_to_be_known_through burlesques [in the coming generation] Shakspere is said to be falsely reputed to be known by the English people in the present generation. The unit predicts that the next generation may know him chiefly through burlesques and that his plays may acquire a new life as pantomimes.

l: excessive deference (Hinze's behavior), Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Hinze’s excessive deference is a habitual, studious and deliberate insincerity: make-believe reverence without deep motive or a calculated search for patronage. It unfolds through lowered voice, downcast eyes, hat handling, worshipful tones, compliments, grand questions, inflated commonplace opinions, and eager attention to Tulpian and others’ authority, without sneering or backbiting.

l: insincerity (social intercourse), Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Insincerity in social intercourse is a common incidental frailty: people may seek to be agreeable, avoid offense, lack exact words, or fill gaps with familiar opinions. Little unpremeditated insincerity merits lenience, but deliberate, studied, persistent make-believe, especially without appetite, purpose, or admiration, deserves impatience.

l: temper, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Temper is primarily the proportion and mode in which qualities are mingled, and commonly an habitual state or general tendency. Popular judgment may excuse bad temper as separate from character, yet it can cause rude, cruel, inconsistent, and unjust behaviour, disrupting healthy mental habits and harmony among perception, conviction, and impulse.

l: Touchwood, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Touchwood is generally regarded as a good fellow, honourable gentleman, steadfast friend, defender of the oppressed, and affectionate-hearted person with high character, gifts, and abilities. Yet his chronic, severe, capricious, pugnacious temper dominates his conduct: he is insolent, quarrelsome, haughty, neglectful, antagonistic, harsh without provocation, and inconsistently opposed even to benevolent measures he sympathizes with. Though thought capable of excellent public service or a great book, his temper makes intimacy insupportable and raises doubt that he could preserve sound judgment and integrity as a public man.

l: character, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: High character requires reliable, principled habits: good feelings and deeds cannot outweigh repeated unjust, rude, cruel, or unreliable conduct, and it likely cannot coexist with a temper like Touchwood's.

l: bad-tempered man, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: A bad-tempered man may have good feelings, do good deeds, and be fundamentally well disposed, yet repeated temper makes his conduct ugly and undermines character. Apologies, amends, friendliness, and promises cannot erase injuries; only a substantial lasting benefit to present and future generations could compensate.

l: public man, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: A public man, especially one like Touchwood, is vulnerable to partisanship when temper drives speech. An uncontrolled temper can make facts and questions serve impulsive attitudes, enslave honesty, and compel defense of insults or contradictory opinions; public life is therefore especially hazardous.

l: Parliament, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_a setting for public speaking [in public life] The unit rejects the hope that Touchwood should be elected to Parliament and use his abilities to serve his country there. It argues that frequent speaking in Parliament would make it difficult for him to preserve integrity of opinion and avoid discreditable partisanship.

l: public life, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: requires integrity of opinion [especially in parliamentary or platform speaking] Public life would expose Touchwood's capricious temper to consequences more serious than the inconsistencies it currently produces in private life. His words, once spoken in a bitter or contradictory mood, could create a public necessity to justify them through later opinions and acts.

l: society, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Society grows through fellowship, orderly self-interest, public conscience, relations between the sexes, sensitivity to others’ claims, and socially useful work; it is threatened by selfishness, oppression, dishonesty, malicious journalism, political partiality, and lax workmanship.

l: partisanship, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Partisanship is a temper-driven adherence to opinion before evidence, then justification afterward, potentially compromising judgment, integrity, and consistency in public careers.

l: Touchwood's great book, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Touchwood’s great book is an expected comprehensive work that would preserve his best self and benefit society. Though everyone believes him capable, his powers remain unproven; perhaps his love of disappointing expectations has kept the book unwritten.

l: apology and amends, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Apology and amends are excessive, artificial compensation after habitual offensiveness. Though better deeds may be remembered without malice, they unfold as penance for prior offences and cannot restore confidence, erase discomfort, or compensate the injured person.

l: Spike, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Spike is a wealthy cotton manufacturer, elector, and self-styled Liberal who votes for Progress, strongly supports the Reform Bill and repeal of the Corn Laws, and favors foreign markets. Trade is central: he understands his own affairs, resists legislation that hampers them, and becomes public-spirited because his economic interests coincide with those of his neighbours, making him a representative of class needs rather than a radical. He is tall, cleanly, abstemious, and melancholy, with leisure-born ennui after making his fortune. Though he aspires to intellectual society, keeps an orderly library, and welcomes beneficed clergymen, his knowledge is limited and his mind resists it. He might have become a member of Parliament or Government under different birth and eligibility conditions.

l: Progress, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_a abstraction [worshipped under many specific names and forms] Progress is an abstraction with many specific names and forms of activity. Spike serves Progress through spinning and weaving and votes on its side, although he does not consciously identify himself with Progress under that name.

l: spinning and weaving, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_a form of Progress [manufacturing and wholesale] Spinning and weaving are presented as the chief manufacturing and wholesale form through which Spike has unconsciously served Progress from his early years.

l: cotton manufacture, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_a trade [managed by Spike] Cotton manufacture enabled Spike to make his fortune and attain the chief object of his ambition. His understanding of the trade also made him recognize that an enlarged market for his business required the enlargement of his neighbours' markets.

l: Reform Bill, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: supports large trading towns [granting them representation] The Reform Bill gave Spike a strong political opinion. He believed that the large trading towns ought to send members, and portraits of the Reform heroes hung in his library.

l: Liberalism, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Liberalism is represented through Spike's pride in being a Liberal. His support reflects his views on the Reform Bill and trade rather than a broad or deeply examined set of political principles.

l: Repeal of the Corn Laws, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Spike was thoroughly convinced of the Repeal of the Corn Laws. He believed that foreign people from whom corn was taken might then be able to buy cotton goods they had previously gone without.

l: Corn Laws, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: The Corn Laws are connected with Spike's concern for foreign markets. Their repeal appeared to him capable of expanding the market for cotton goods.

l: legislation, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: causes common injury and common benefit [through shared effects on traders] Spike objects to items of legislation when they hamper his own trade. Because the same legislation hampers his neighbours' trade, his demand for change becomes a shared political demand rather than merely a selfish one.

l: Mordax, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Mordax is an admirable man: ardent in intellectual work, public-spirited, affectionate, and able to convey ingenious ideas and elevated feeling through well-chosen words. He is kindly, conscientious, generous, and tender toward a suffering friend outside special temptations. Yet he resists admitting error and welcomes neither novelty nor ideas he did not discover. When contradiction or correction threatens his fiery self-respect, arrogant egoism inflames him into self-justifying unscrupulousness, cruelty, and polemical rudeness.

l: Acer, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Acer is a speaker and moral critic who questions asserted virtues, judging fairness and goodwill by tender use of public influence toward overlooked, disadvantaged people.

l: Laniger, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Laniger has temper but no talent for repartee; after Mordax fiercely attacks him verbally, he is hurt and concludes Mordax is a wolf at heart while friends fail to grasp his pain.

l: Dante, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Dante is a precise yet imaginative seer who distinguishes entranced vision from ordinary external fact. His strongest insight joins sustained creative energy to sane expectation; he also expresses a sentiment on courtesy and villainy and places Judas at Malebolge’s bottom.

l: The Watch-Dog of Knowledge, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_a unit of a longer document The Watch-Dog of Knowledge is the title of this unit, which considers the dangers of guarding inquiry through arrogant correction and cruel exclusion. The unit argues that the defense of truth should be restrained by fairness, kindness, and fellow-feeling toward contemporaries.

l: self-respect, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: demands advantage over Mordax [only monarchs of thought may have it] Mordax's self-respect is described as fiery and as demanding that only monarchs of thought should have an advantage over him. When threatened by correction or contradiction, it contributes to his refusal to admit error and to his cruelty.

l: moral tests, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Acer's moral tests judge justice and benevolence by whether public figures tenderly recognize disadvantaged, overlooked claimants' undefended claims, though the narrator warns these tests may be delusive.

l: intellect, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Intellect is domain-specific rather than uniform: excellence or intense specialization in one field may coexist with, or even hinder, competence in another.

l: moral nature, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: can_contain fine impulses and cruel actions [when particular temptations inflame egoism] A person's moral nature is not to be judged by its weakest point any more than intellect is. Kindly and generous dispositions may coexist with unfair or cruel actions in situations that peculiarly inflame egoism.

l: truth and justice, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: are_invoked_as justifications for cruelty [by angry people seeking to hurt others] Truth and justice are invoked by Mordax as reasons for scourging incompetent or presumptuous intruders. The unit warns that such elevated motives can disguise cruelty and insists that fairness and kindness toward the person immediately concerned must be considered first.

l: polemical rudeness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_compatible_with kindly and generous moral nature [under special temptation] Mordax's conscience is active in some relationships but does not trouble him over his polemical rudeness and brutality. He can leave the care of a sick friend and immediately write a merciless rejoinder against someone who challenges his intellectual authority.

l: humility, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_appreciated_by self-satisfied people [more than by diffident people] Humility is presented as an admission of error and a frank welcome of ideas not previously present in one's mind. Pummel lacks this quality, since he cannot acknowledge being newly informed, while self-satisfied people are especially eager to expose conceit in others.

l: Mixtus, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Mixtus is a wealthy commercial man whose growing wealth supports a London mansion kept as a little palace and liberal spending. Known among fashionable acquaintances as a rich man, he chiefly distinguishes himself through genial hospitality and usefulness. In youth he was religious and philanthropic, visiting the poor as an exhorter and helper and attending Mr Apollos’s lectures; he later married Scintilla despite opposing ideals. He values knowledge and collects works on colonisation, supports commerce and sometimes war as means to spread Christianity, and retains private, bashful religion and benevolence. Success leaves him divided, uncertain, and bitter toward obstructive workers.

l: Scintilla, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Scintilla is a pretty, lively, musical, socially adept woman married to Mixtus for the advantages of being a rich man’s wife. She gathers fashionable society, associates with wealthy Greek merchant families and artists, and treats religious, social, and philosophical seriousness as absurd or dull, hoping to laugh Mixtus out of bachelor habits.

l: Mr Apollos, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_a congregational preacher [eloquent and liberal-minded] Mr Apollos is an eloquent Congregational preacher who studied in Germany and held liberal, advanced views beyond the ordinary teaching of his sect. Mixtus attended his lectures for young men and once regarded his teaching as part of his religious and intellectual formation.

l: wealth and money, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Wealth and money enable social dominance in Mixtus's adopted world. As Mixtus grows richer, he sees money as the chief means to obtain the best things, yet still affirms mind and genius, leaving an unresolved alternation.

l: commercial success, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: increases Mixtus's wealth [through business ability and rewarded exertion] Mixtus’s ability in business and growing commercial success help draw him toward Scintilla and the London world of wealth. His commercial position ultimately becomes the main category by which others judge him, despite his knowledge and former aspirations.

l: religion, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: is_private_to Mixtus [because his public position is incompatible with it] Mixtus once had strong religious principles and yearnings, attended Mr Apollos’s lectures, and worked among the poor. He has not wholly abandoned religion, but he feels bashful about his former faith and keeps it private because his current position and avowed objects seem incompatible with public acknowledgment.

l: Christianity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: Christianity is an expanded religion, born through Jewish separateness, with a substantial genealogy and an asserted claim to surpass the spiritual doctrine of the Hebrew prophets. It is presented as having determined the religion of half the world, though modern praise often disowns its Jewish origin. The records condemn its use to justify vengeance, persecution, greed, and cruelty against the Jews. In Mixtus's theory, Christianity spreads through commercial intercourse, even with war as a possible pioneer.

l: religious and social reform, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
s: motivates Mixtus [during his youth] As a young man, Mixtus expected to use his future wealth chiefly for religious and reforming purposes and held strongly democratic views concerning aristocratic and landed privilege. He retains benevolence and helps the needy, the clever, and the industrious, but his commercial responsibilities increasingly produce bitterness toward obstructive workers.
